summary: Research, verify and chain 40 quotes on: be prepared, keep the body and mind ready, every day is new; Ashtanga is the tool

chains.title: Carousel 1: Just in Case (central image: young Bernstein reading the music the night before the call came)

lines.line: You don't know what today will bring. Nobody does. So now what?
Heat and cold, joy and pain: they come and go. Meet them bravely.
Bernstein, 25, studied the music just in case. Next day, he led the orchestra.
Was he lucky? Chance only helps the mind that is already prepared.
Prepared how? Japanese sport trains three as one: mind, skill, body.
Body first: eight weeks of yoga went with more strength and flexibility.
Then the mind: ups and downs touch it, but it does not tremble.
Built speck by speck: gather dust, and you get a mountain.
Guruji said: practise without fail, and body, mind and spirit grow happy.
Your morning mat is your 'just in case.' Ashtanga works quietly, slowly but surely.

chains.title: Carousel 2: The Sledge in Summer (central image: a sledge made ready in summer, months before the snow)

lines.line: Even the sun is new every day. Today has never happened before.
Good news: bouncing back is not rare. It is made of ordinary, everyday strengths.
So build them early: ready your sledge in summer, your cart in winter.
Ants know it too: small, not strong, yet they store food in summer.
At 15, Amundsen trained in the snow every free day, years before his adventures.
Strong, but not stiff: the willow bends under snow and does not break.
Then the mind: whatever comes, keep doing your work, steady and brave.
The Buddha's last words: everything changes, so keep practising with care.
Missed a day? In one study, one miss did not spoil the habit.
Morning Ashtanga is your summer sledge. Practise for years: peace is coming. No problem.

chains.title: Carousel 3: The Snapped String (central image: a violin string snapping mid-concert while the music goes on)

lines.line: At 14, strings snapped on two violins mid-concert. Midori never missed a note.
Strings snap. Joy and sorrow both come. Accept them with a calm, content mind.
How did she stay calm? Prepare ahead, and there is nothing to worry about.
An old Thai saying: buy a buffalo at ploughing time, and you pay more.
Start with the body: asana should be firm, and pleasant too.
Then the mind. Hancock hit a wrong chord. Miles breathed and made it right.
More things scare us than hurt us. We suffer more in our heads.
Same place, most days: in one study, habits like this went with less stress.
Yoga is 99 percent practice, 1 percent theory, Guruji said. So live it daily.
Sting: after morning Ashtanga, more energy, more done, a calmer mind. Your turn tomorrow.

chains.title: Carousel 4: The Astronaut's Secret (central image: astronauts practising things going wrong, on the ground, before launch)

lines.line: Every day is a good day. Even the one you never saw coming.
Maybe you'll eat, maybe you'll fast. Guruji said: each morning, wake up and practise.
So train on the calm days, and you stay steady when hard ones come.
Why? Pain that has not come yet is pain you can still avoid.
Wally Funk kept body and mind ready. At 82, she finally flew to space.
Astronauts practise things going wrong, again and again. So when it happens, no panic.
Japan has a word for it: heijoshin, the everyday mind that does not waver.
Keep planting seeds, morning and evening. You never know which one will grow.
A day's plan lies in its morning. A life's plan lies in steady effort.
One Ashtanga student said: practice makes me readier for whatever life throws.

final.checks:
I ran a script over all 40 lines. Results: 40 ids, all different, none outside the verified list. Every line is 14 words or fewer (the longest are exactly 14). No long dash or en dash appears, and the word "pose" is never used ("asana" is used in Y5). Y1 is used and C1 is left out, because they are the same Yunmen quote.

ARC: every carousel walks unknown_day, then prepare_before, body_ready, mind_ready, daily_practice and ashtanga_tool in order:
- Carousel 1: u u p p b b m d d a
- Carousel 2: u u p p b b m d d a
- Carousel 3: u u p p b m m d d a
- Carousel 4: u u p p b m m d a a
Slide 10 always names Ashtanga or the practice and points to the morning:
- 'Your morning mat is your just in case'
- 'Morning Ashtanga is your summer sledge'
- Sting's 'Your turn tomorrow'
- 'readier for whatever life throws', set up by C12's 'a day's plan lies in its morning'. This line echoes Boonchu's 'you don't know what will hit you'.

HOOKS:
- a hard truth plus an open question (W1, 'So now what?')
- a surprise ('Today has never happened before')
- a true story (Midori's strings snapping)
- a contrarian line ('Even the one you never saw coming')

AUTHORS: no author appears twice in a carousel.
- Pattabhi Jois is used once per carousel: A10, A11 and A1. A9 is Sharath reporting Jois, so it sits in carousel 3, which has neither Jois nor Sharath.
- Sharath: A12 in carousel 1, A9 in carousel 3.
- Krishnamacharya: A7 in carousel 2, A2 in carousel 3.
- Patanjali: Y5 in carousel 3, Y3 in carousel 4.
- The Buddha: Y7 in carousel 1, Y10 in carousel 2.
- Seneca: W8 in carousel 3, W3 in carousel 4.
- Book of Proverbs: W1 in carousel 1, W4 in carousel 2.

LANES: every carousel has yoga text, Ashtanga lineage, an Asian or Russian proverb, a Western quote, a true story and a science line. Each also mixes Indian, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Thai, Russian, Greek, Roman, Hebrew and American voices. The Thai (C5), Russian (C4) and Chinese (C3, C12, Y1) items are spread so each audience sees itself.

SCIENCE: B6 and B10 say 'went with'. B9 reports a finding of no effect ('did not spoil'). B2 makes no causal claim. B12 is framed as one student's own words. Nothing says 'causes'.

IMAGERY: no war, accident, flood, storm, rain or water images. I left out C2 and B5 because they are about falling, and W9 because it is a wrestling image. Snow, willow, seeds, a mountain, the sun and a sledge carry the images instead. The tone stays warm and never fear-based. Y3 is framed as 'you can still avoid'; W8 is framed as reassurance.

EDITORIAL GRAFTS AND FIXES:
- Carousel 1 is Draft B's 'Just in Case', with the hook and the callback ending kept. W5 is moved in from Draft A ('Was he lucky?'), which pulls straight out of the Bernstein story. C7 'Prepared how?' bridges into the body slides. S7 is moved out to carousel 4. S3 is rewritten so a stranger knows what happened ('Next day, he led the orchestra'), with 'scores' made plainer as 'music'. Y7 is clarified ('ups and downs touch it, but it does not tremble').
- Carousel 2 is Draft A's snow motif (sledge, Amundsen, willow) with Draft B's ant and B9 'Missed a day?' added. B2 is bridged into C4 ('So build them early'). The ending calls back the sledge and keeps Guruji's 'No problem'. Repeats of 'steady' and 'Even' were cut.
- Carousel 3 is Draft B's 'Snapped String', with A2 made more faithful ('Accept', santosha). B4 and W5 were swapped out to make room for the Thai buffalo idiom (C5) and Seneca W8. W8 follows Miles's wrong chord naturally. A9 is placed here so the Jois/Sharath rule holds. Draft A's C5 line ran to 15 words in my rewrite, so I cut it to 14.
- Carousel 4 is Draft A's astronaut spine. A1 is at slide 2 instead of B2. S7 is tightened ('again and again ... no panic'). C9 heijoshin replaces C8 and links to the astronauts' calm. W10 and C12 set up the morning before the B12 close.

DROPPED LINES: I dropped two weak lines from the drafts:
- Draft A's W11 Thoreau line, which is about simple living, not practice.
- Draft B's 'Tomorrow?' ending, which landed flat.

UNUSED: 29 verified items are left unused and ready for a fifth or sixth carousel: A3, A4, A5, A6, A8, B1, B3, B4, B7, B11, C8, C11, S4, S9, S10, S11, W6, W7, W11, W12, Y6, Y8, Y9, Y11 and Y12. Also unused, but set aside on purpose: C1 (duplicate of Y1), C2 and B5 (falling imagery), and W9 (wrestling).

rows.line: You don't know what today will bring. Nobody does. So now what?
rows.quote: Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.
rows.source: Proverbs 27:1, King James Version, 1611 (standard 1769 text, Bible Gateway)

rows.line: Heat and cold, joy and pain: they come and go. Meet them bravely.
rows.quote: The contacts of matter, O son of Kuntî, giving cold and heat, pleasure and pain, they come and go, impermanent; endure them bravely, O Bhârata.
rows.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14, tr. Annie Besant, The Bhagavad-Gita, 4th ed., 1922 (Wikisource transcription of the scanned edition, printed p. 24)

rows.line: Bernstein, 25, studied the music just in case. Next day, he led the orchestra.
rows.who: Leonard Bernstein, aged 25, assistant conductor of the New York Philharmonic, 14 November 1943
rows.quote: The possibility seemed remote, and the young man went to a song recital. When he got home, however, he decided to look over the scores of the Philharmonic program 'just in case.'
rows.source: 'Young Aide Leads Philharmonic, Steps In When Bruno Walter Is Ill', The New York Times, 15 November 1943 (unsigned; front page per Smithsonian Magazine, Marissa Vonesh, 21 August 2018). Full text reprinted in the Pristine Audio PASC 533 booklet.

rows.line: Was he lucky? Chance only helps the mind that is already prepared.
rows.quote: In the fields of observation, chance only favours the mind which is prepared.
rows.source: Speech at Douai, 7 December 1854, at the formal installation of the Faculté des lettres de Douai and the Faculté des sciences de Lille (Pasteur was the new dean in Lille); Œuvres de Pasteur, t. 7, ed. Pasteur Vallery-Radot, Masson, pp. 129-132. English as in René Vallery-Radot, The Life of Pasteur, ch. IV, tr. Mrs R. L. Devonshire

rows.line: Prepared how? Japanese sport trains three as one: mind, skill, body.
rows.quote: Mind, technique, body.
rows.source: Kotobank, デジタル大辞泉 (Shogakukan), entry 心技体: '精神力（心）・技術（技）・体力（体）の総称。スポーツ界でよく使う。「心技体のバランス」' Literal translation.

rows.line: Body first: eight weeks of yoga went with more strength and flexibility.
rows.who: M. D. Tran, R. G. Holly, J. Lashbrook, E. A. Amsterdam, Department of Exercise Science, University of California at Davis
rows.quote: These findings indicate that regular hatha yoga practice can elicit improvements in the health-related aspects of physical fitness.
rows.source: Tran MD, Holly RG, Lashbrook J, Amsterdam EA. Effects of Hatha Yoga Practice on the Health-Related Aspects of Physical Fitness. Preventive Cardiology, 2001;4(4):165-170. doi:10.1111/j.1520-037x.2001.00542.x. PMID 11832673 (abstract).

rows.line: Then the mind: ups and downs touch it, but it does not tremble.
rows.credit: The Buddha · Sutta Nipata 2.4, tr. Sujato
rows.quote: Though touched by worldly conditions, their mind does not tremble; sorrowless, stainless, secure: this is the highest blessing.
rows.source: Sutta Nipata 2.4 (Mangala Sutta, 'Blessings'), segments 12.1-12.4, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral (CC0)

rows.line: Built speck by speck: gather dust, and you get a mountain.
rows.quote: Gather dust, and you get Mount Tai.
rows.source: Urimalsaem (National Institute of Korean Language), entry 티끌 모아 태산: '아무리 작은 것이라도 모이고 모이면 나중에 큰 덩어리가 됨을 비유적으로 이르는 말.' Synonyms listed: 먼지도 쌓이면 큰 산이 된다, 모래알도 모으면 산이 된다. Literal translation.

rows.line: Guruji said: practise without fail, and body, mind and spirit grow happy.
rows.credit: K. Pattabhi Jois · Yoga Mala, Preface 1997
rows.quote: ...if we practice it without fail, we will then attain physical, mental, and spiritual happiness...
rows.source: Yoga Mala, Preface, signed 'K. Pattabhi Jois, Mysore, September 1997'; English tr. Kadam and Chandrashekar (North Point Press 2002/2010)

rows.line: Your morning mat is your 'just in case.' Ashtanga works quietly, slowly but surely.
rows.quote: Ashtanga Yoga works in quiet ways. ... Through this practice, whatever your reason for starting may be, results will show – if I may use the cliché – slowly, but surely.
rows.source: R. Sharath Jois with Isha Singh Sawhney, Ageless: A Yogi's Secrets to a Long and Healthy Life (Juggernaut Books, 2018), Introduction, p. xvi

rows.line: Even the sun is new every day. Today has never happened before.
rows.quote: The sun is new every day.
rows.source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy, 2nd ed., London: A. & C. Black, 1908, ch. III 'Herakleitos of Ephesos', fragment 32 (= DK 22 B6), preserved in Aristotle, Meteorology II.2, 355a13

rows.line: Good news: bouncing back is not rare. It is made of ordinary, everyday strengths.
rows.who: Ann S. Masten, developmental psychologist, University of Minnesota
rows.quote: ...resilience is made of ordinary rather than extraordinary processes...
rows.source: Masten AS. Ordinary magic: Resilience processes in development. American Psychologist, 2001;56(3):227-238. doi:10.1037/0003-066X.56.3.227. PMID 11315249 (abstract).

rows.line: So build them early: ready your sledge in summer, your cart in winter.
rows.quote: Get your sledge ready in summer, and your cart in winter.
rows.source: V. I. Dal, Poslovitsy russkogo naroda (Proverbs of the Russian People), 1862 (academic.ru text of the 1989 edition), cross-referenced to the rubric ПРИЛИЧИЕ — ВЕЖЕСТВО — ОБЫЧАЙ. Literal translation. Modern form: 'Готовь сани летом, а телегу зимой'.

rows.line: Ants know it too: small, not strong, yet they store food in summer.
rows.who: Book of Proverbs (Hebrew Bible), words of Agur
rows.quote: There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise: The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer.
rows.source: Proverbs 30:24-25, King James Version, 1611 (standard 1769 text, Bible Gateway)

rows.line: At 15, Amundsen trained in the snow every free day, years before his adventures.
rows.credit: Roald Amundsen · My Life as an Explorer
rows.who: Roald Amundsen, recalling his teenage years in Norway (from age 15)
rows.quote: I began at once to fit myself for this career... At every opportunity of freedom from school, from November to April, I went out in the open... increasing my skill in traversing ice and snow and hardening my muscles for the coming great adventure.
rows.source: Roald Amundsen, My Life as an Explorer, ch. 1 'Early Memories', p. 3 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, Page & Co., 1927). Public domain in the US since 2023.

rows.line: Strong, but not stiff: the willow bends under snow and does not break.
rows.quote: The willow does not break under snow.
rows.source: Kotobank, デジタル大辞泉 (Shogakukan): '柳の枝はよくしなうので雪の重みで折れることはない。柔らかいものは、堅いものよりかえってよく持ちこたえるというたとえ。' Literal translation.

rows.line: Then the mind: whatever comes, keep doing your work, steady and brave.
rows.quote: Whatever hurdles arise to your happiness or welfare, to continue to undertake with mental steadfastness and courage whatever work that has to be done is dhrthi.
rows.source: Yoga Makaranda (Kannada ed. 1934; Tamil ed. 1938), ch. 2.1 'Yama and Niyama', yama no. 6, p. 22; English tr. Lakshmi Ranganathan and Nandini Ranganathan, 2006

rows.line: The Buddha's last words: everything changes, so keep practising with care.
rows.credit: The Buddha · Digha Nikaya 16, tr. Sujato
rows.quote: Conditions fall apart. Persist with diligence.
rows.source: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), segment 6.7.3 (also 3.51.4), tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral, 2018 (CC0)

rows.line: Missed a day? In one study, one miss did not spoil the habit.
rows.credit: Lally et al. · Eur J Soc Psychol, 2010
rows.who: Phillippa Lally, Cornelia H. M. van Jaarsveld, Henry W. W. Potts, Jane Wardle, University College London
rows.quote: Missing one opportunity to perform the behaviour did not materially affect the habit formation process.
rows.source: Lally P, van Jaarsveld CHM, Potts HWW, Wardle J. How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010;40(6):998-1009 (online 16 July 2009). doi:10.1002/ejsp.674.

rows.line: Morning Ashtanga is your summer sledge. Practise for years: peace is coming. No problem.
rows.credit: Pattabhi Jois · recalled by Kino MacGregor
rows.who: K. Pattabhi Jois, as recalled by his student Kino MacGregor
rows.quote: You take it practice many years, then shanti [peace] is coming…no problem.
rows.source: Kino MacGregor, section 'Peace is coming, no problem.' in 'Remembrances of K. Pattabhi Jois', Yoga Journal (datePublished 29 Oct 2009 in page metadata; page shows 'Updated January 14, 2025'). The exchange was in Mysore when she was 22, on her first trip.

rows.line: At 14, strings snapped on two violins mid-concert. Midori never missed a note.
rows.who: Midori (Goto), violinist, aged 14, playing Bernstein's Serenade at Tanglewood with the Boston Symphony Orchestra, Leonard Bernstein conducting, 1986
rows.quote: The concertmaster handed Midori his full-size violin, which she played until a string on that broke as well... She never missed a note.
rows.source: Evelyn Velleman, news post on Midori's official website, 28 November 2023. Supported by WAMC (Joe Donahue, 17 August 2018) and the Boston Globe (7 November 2025), which both describe the string breaking twice and the borrowed violins.

rows.line: Strings snap. Joy and sorrow both come. Accept them with a calm, content mind.
rows.quote: The sorrows and pleasure that result from any occurrences due to variations of time and place — to accept these with a peaceful, contented mind is santosha.
rows.source: Yoga Makaranda (Kannada ed. 1934; Tamil ed. 1938), ch. 2.1 'Yama and Niyama', niyama no. 2, p. 23; English tr. Lakshmi Ranganathan and Nandini Ranganathan (translators' note dated 15 Oct 2006), from the Tamil edition

rows.line: How did she stay calm? Prepare ahead, and there is nothing to worry about.
rows.credit: 有備無患 · Chinese, Japanese, Korean idiom
rows.who: Chinese idiom, also a Japanese proverb and a Korean idiom
rows.quote: Have preparation, have no worry. (Japanese: If you are prepared, there is nothing to worry about.)
rows.source: Kotobank, 故事成語を知る辞典, entry 備えあれば憂いなし: '平生からいざというときの準備を怠らなければ、万一の事態が起こっても、少しも心配することはない'. Standard Korean Language Dictionary (National Institute of Korean Language), entry 유비-무환(有備無患): '미리 준비가 되어 있으면 걱정할 것이 없음.' Literal translation.

rows.line: An old Thai saying: buy a buffalo at ploughing time, and you pay more.
rows.quote: Buy a buffalo at ploughing time, buy cloth at New Year.
rows.source: Thai Wiktionary, entry ซื้อควายหน้านา ซื้อผ้าหน้าตรุษ, marked (สำ) idiom: 'ซื้อของไม่คำนึงถึงกาลเวลา ย่อมได้ของราคาแพง' / 'ทำอะไรไม่เหมาะกับกาลเวลาย่อมได้รับความเดือดร้อน' (buy without regard to the season and you pay a high price; do things at the wrong time and you get into trouble). The same definition appears in TruePlookpanya's Thai idiom list (https://www.trueplookpanya.com/blogdiary/26692). Variants: ซื้อวัวหน้านา ซื้อผ้าหน้าหนาว / ซื้อควายหน้านา ซื้อผ้าหน้าหนาว. Literal translation. The definition wording is the one usually credited to the Royal Institute dictionary, but I could not open ORST to confirm it.

rows.line: Start with the body: asana should be firm, and pleasant too.
rows.quote: Posture is that which is firm and pleasant.
rows.source: Yoga Sutra 2.46, tr. Swami Vivekananda, Raja Yoga (1896), in The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1 (Wikisource)

rows.line: Then the mind. Hancock hit a wrong chord. Miles breathed and made it right.
rows.who: Herbie Hancock, jazz pianist, on playing in Miles Davis's band
rows.quote: I played this chord that was so wrong... And Miles just took a breath and he played some notes that made my chord right.
rows.source: Interview with Norah O'Donnell, CBS This Morning, in 'Jazz legend Herbie Hancock on his career and future', CBS News, 25 December 2013.

rows.line: More things scare us than hurt us. We suffer more in our heads.
rows.credit: Seneca · Letters to Lucilius 13, tr. Gummere
rows.quote: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
rows.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 13 ('On groundless fears'), section 4, tr. Richard M. Gummere, Loeb Classical Library vol. I, 1917

rows.line: Same place, most days: in one study, habits like this went with less stress.
rows.credit: Wood et al. · J Pers Soc Psychol, 2002
rows.who: Wendy Wood, Jeffrey M. Quinn, Deborah A. Kashy, Texas A&M University
rows.quote: ...the self-regulatory benefits of habits were apparent in the lesser feelings of stress associated with habitual than nonhabitual behavior.
rows.source: Wood W, Quinn JM, Kashy DA. Habits in everyday life: thought, emotion, and action. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2002;83(6):1281-1297. doi:10.1037/0022-3514.83.6.1281. PMID 12500811 (abstract).

rows.line: Yoga is 99 percent practice, 1 percent theory, Guruji said. So live it daily.
rows.credit: R. Sharath Jois · Yoga Mala foreword, 2009
rows.who: R. Sharath Jois, reporting K. Pattabhi Jois's frequent saying
rows.quote: "Yoga is ninety-nine percent practice and one percent theory" is an idea that Guruji repeatedly presented. He meant that ... we must engage it practically in our daily life.
rows.source: R. Sharath, Foreword to Yoga Mala (North Point Press, 2010 edition), signed 'R. Sharath, Mysore, October 12, 2009'

rows.line: Sting: after morning Ashtanga, more energy, more done, a calmer mind. Your turn tomorrow.
rows.who: Sting, musician, on the Ashtanga vinyasa series he learned from Danny Paradise
rows.quote: When I really do my Yoga in the morning, I have more energy in the day. I get more done. My mind is more composed.
rows.source: Sting in conversation with Ganga White, 'Ganga speaks with Sting about Yoga & his life', White Lotus Foundation website. Undated on that page. The internal clues ('the past four years' of practice, 'It's not going to end in 1999') point to the mid-1990s, and sting.com archives an 'Interview: YOGA JOURNAL (1995)' that comes up for this exact sentence. I could not open the sting.com page.

rows.line: Every day is a good day. Even the one you never saw coming.
rows.quote: Every day is a good day.
rows.source: Blue Cliff Record (Biyan Lu 碧巖錄), case 6, compiled with commentary by Yuanwu Keqin, 1125. The English is a literal translation of the Chinese; no published translation was used.

rows.line: Maybe you'll eat, maybe you'll fast. Guruji said: each morning, wake up and practise.
rows.credit: Pattabhi Jois · recalled by David Williams
rows.who: K. Pattabhi Jois, as recalled by his student David Williams (Manju Jois translating)
rows.quote: Each morning, wake up. Do as much yoga as you want. Maybe you'll eat, maybe you'll fast. Maybe you'll sleep indoors, maybe you'll sleep outdoors... Practice yoga, and all is coming!
rows.source: David Williams, 'Big Yogi, Little Yogi', in 'Remembrances of K. Pattabhi Jois', Yoga Journal (YJ Editors; datePublished 29 Oct 2009 in page metadata; page shows 'Updated January 14, 2025'). Conversation on the last night of Jois's 1975 visit to Encinitas, California.

rows.line: So train on the calm days, and you stay steady when hard ones come.
rows.credit: Seneca · Letters to Lucilius 18, tr. Gummere
rows.quote: It is precisely in times of immunity from care that the soul should toughen itself beforehand for occasions of greater stress... If you would not have a man flinch when the crisis comes, train him before it comes.
rows.source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 18 ('On festivals and fasting'), section 6, tr. Richard M. Gummere, Loeb Classical Library vol. I, 1917

rows.line: Why? Pain that has not come yet is pain you can still avoid.
rows.quote: The misery which is not yet come is to be avoided.
rows.source: Yoga Sutra 2.16, tr. Swami Vivekananda, Raja Yoga (1896), in The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1 (Wikisource)

rows.line: Wally Funk kept body and mind ready. At 82, she finally flew to space.
rows.who: Wally Funk, pilot and Mercury 13 trainee, speaking at StoryCorps in Dallas, 2017
rows.quote: I never let anything stop me. I know that my body and my mind can take anything that any space outfit wants to give me.
rows.source: StoryCorps conversation with Mary Holsenbeck, Dallas, 2017, broadcast in John White, 'Wally Funk, A Lifelong Aspiring Astronaut, Will Finally Head To Space At 82', NPR Morning Edition, 9 July 2021. Record: Guinness World Records, oldest person in space (female), 82 years 169 days, Blue Origin NS-16, 2021.

rows.line: Astronauts practise things going wrong, again and again. So when it happens, no panic.
rows.who: Chris Hadfield, Canadian astronaut, on his 2001 spacewalk when anti-fog solution got into his eyes
rows.quote: And we don't just practice things going right, we practice things going wrong all the time... And even if you're blinded, your natural, panicky reaction doesn't happen.
rows.source: Chris Hadfield, 'What I learned from going blind in space', TED2014, Vancouver, recorded 18 March 2014 (official TED transcript).

rows.line: Japan has a word for it: heijoshin, the everyday mind that does not waver.
rows.quote: Heijōshin: the everyday mind, a state of mind that does not waver.
rows.source: Kotobank. デジタル大辞泉: 'ふだんと変わらない心。揺れ動くことのない心理状態。' 精選版 日本国語大辞典 marks the Buddhist reading びょうじょうしん (仏語) and cites Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō, 身心学道 (1231-53), and 無門関 case 19. Literal translation.

rows.line: Keep planting seeds, morning and evening. You never know which one will grow.
rows.quote: In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good.
rows.source: Ecclesiastes 11:6, King James Version, 1611 (standard 1769 text, Bible Gateway)

rows.line: A day's plan lies in its morning. A life's plan lies in steady effort.
rows.who: Traditional Chinese saying, in the Zengguang Xianwen (anonymous collection of sayings, first named in the late Ming and expanded in the Ming and Qing)
rows.quote: ...the plan for a day lies in the morning; ... the plan for a life lies in diligence.
rows.source: Zengguang Xianwen (增廣昔時賢文), part 1 (上集), saying no. 44 in the Chinese Wikisource text. Literal translation of the full line: 'The plan for a year lies in spring, the plan for a day lies in the morning; the plan for a family lies in harmony, the plan for a life lies in diligence.' Dating per zh.wikipedia 增廣賢文: the title first appears in the Ming Wanli era, the text was expanded by Ming and Qing writers, and the author is unknown.

rows.line: One Ashtanga student said: practice makes me readier for whatever life throws.
rows.who: An anonymous regular Ashtanga practitioner, quoted in a study by Daniela Ramirez-Duran, Margaret L. Kern and Helen Stokes, University of Melbourne
rows.quote: I strongly believe that my yoga practice makes me a better person and more equipped to deal with the challenges that life throws at us.
rows.source: Ramirez-Duran D, Kern ML, Stokes H. From practice to lifestyle: conceptualizations of yoga in regular Ashtanga yoga practitioners using reflexive thematic analysis. Frontiers in Psychology, 2025;16:1582275 (online 4 June 2025). doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1582275. PMC12177368 (Results).

flags.problem: Added claim. Daijisen only says 心技体 is a collective term for mental strength, technique and physical strength that is often used in sports. It says nothing about how Japanese sport 'trains' them or trains them 'as one'.
flags.new_line: Prepared how? Japanese sport has one word for three things: mind, skill, body.

flags.problem: Unclear English. In English, 'gather dust' is a fixed idiom meaning 'sit unused and neglected', which says the opposite of daily practice and will confuse learners. The meaning in Urimalsaem (tiny things pile up into something big) is otherwise correct.
flags.new_line: Speck by speck: pile up dust, and you get a mountain.

flags.problem: Calm is sourced (the Midori site says 'display of calm'). But the question and answer together claim she stayed calm because she prepared ahead. No source says that about Midori. It puts an unsourced reason on a real person. The idiom itself is verified (Kotobank, from the Shujing).
flags.new_line: The lesson? Prepare ahead, and there is nothing to worry about.

flags.problem: Seneca 13.4 (Gummere) says 'we suffer more OFTEN in imagination than in reality'. 'We suffer more in our heads' drops 'often' and says more than what, so it reads as stronger suffering, not more frequent suffering. A learner could also read 'suffer in our heads' as head pain. The fix keeps Seneca's meaning in plain words.
flags.new_line: More things scare us than hurt us. We often suffer only in our minds.

flags.problem: The abstract defines habits as behaviour 'performed almost daily in stable contexts'. 'Most days' is looser than 'almost daily', so the stress finding is stretched to a wider group than the study covered. 'Went with' (associated) is the right strength. The credit is right.
flags.new_line: Almost daily, same place: in one study, habits like this went with less stress.

flags.problem: The source is verified: Blue Cliff Record case 6, 日日是好日. But 'the one you never saw coming' is an English idiom a learner may not follow: read literally, every day 'comes'. The fix says the same thing in plain words.
flags.new_line: Every day is a good day. Even a day that surprises you.

flags.problem: NPR (9 July 2021) quotes her: 'I know that my body and my mind can take anything.' The age of 82 is right. 'Kept body and mind ready' adds a claim that she kept herself in training over the years, and the source does not say that. The fix stays with what she said.
flags.new_line: Wally Funk said her body and mind were ready. At 82, she reached space.

flags.problem: The definition is verified (Daijisen: 揺れ動くことのない心理状態, a state of mind that does not sway). But 'waver' is advanced vocabulary (around CEFR C1/C2), not plain English for a 10-year-old learner. 'Does not shake' is the literal sense.
flags.new_line: Japan has a word for it: heijoshin, the everyday mind that does not shake.

flags.problem: The quote is verified in PMC12177368: 'more equipped to deal with the challenges that life throws at us.' The line's 'readier for whatever life throws' cuts the idiom short (no object, 'throws' alone). 'Whatever' widens 'challenges' to anything at all. 'Readier' is an unusual word for learners. The slide still lands on Ashtanga.
flags.new_line: One Ashtanga student said: practice makes me better at facing life's challenges.

judged.why: Daijisen only defines 心技体 as a collective term for mind, technique and body that is often used in sport. 'Trains three as one' adds a claim about how Japanese sport trains, and no source says that. The fixed line keeps to the dictionary meaning (13 words).
judged.final_line: Prepared how? Japanese sport has one word for three things: mind, skill, body.

judged.why: In English, 'gather dust' means 'sit unused and neglected', which is the opposite of daily practice and would confuse learners. 'Pile up dust' keeps the Urimalsaem meaning (small things add up to something big) without the idiom (11 words).
judged.final_line: Speck by speck: pile up dust, and you get a mountain.

judged.why: The question and answer together give a real person (Midori) a reason for her calm, preparing ahead, and no source supports that. The credit is for the idiom, not for her. Framing it as a general lesson removes the unsourced cause and keeps the verified idiom (11 words).
judged.final_line: The lesson? Prepare ahead, and there is nothing to worry about.
judged.final_credit: 有備無患 · Chinese, Japanese, Korean idiom

judged.why: Gummere's text reads 'we suffer more OFTEN in imagination than in reality'. Dropping 'often' and the 'than' part turns more frequent suffering into stronger suffering, and 'in our heads' can be read as head pain. The fixer's version adds 'only', which is a small claim of its own. I also left out 'scare', because the safety rules bar fear. Seneca's comparison is kept whole (11 words).
judged.final_line: We suffer more often in our minds than in real life.
judged.final_credit: Seneca · Letters to Lucilius 13, tr. Gummere

judged.why: I checked the PubMed abstract. It defines habits as behaviour 'performed almost daily in stable contexts'. 'Most days' widens that to a group the study did not cover. 'Went with' is the right strength. Fixed line is 14 words.
judged.final_line: Almost daily, same place: in one study, habits like this went with less stress.
judged.final_credit: Wood et al. · J Pers Soc Psychol, 2002

judged.why: The source is verified. 'The one you never saw coming' is an idiom, and a learner reading it literally may not follow it. 'Even a day that surprises you' is plain English. It follows from 'every day', so it adds no new claim for Yunmen (12 words).
judged.final_line: Every day is a good day. Even a day that surprises you.

judged.why: I checked the NPR text. She said 'I know that my body and my mind can take anything', but the article never says she kept training or kept herself ready over the years. 'Kept body and mind ready' adds that claim. The age of 82 matches NPR and Guinness (82 years 169 days). The fixed line reports what she said (14 words).
judged.final_line: Wally Funk said her body and mind were ready. At 82, she reached space.

judged.why: 'Waver' is advanced vocabulary, not plain English for a 10-year-old learner. Daijisen's 揺れ動くことのない (a state of mind that does not sway) comes through faithfully as 'stays steady', which reads more naturally than 'does not shake' (13 words).
judged.final_line: Japan has a word for it: heijoshin, the everyday mind that stays steady.

judged.why: 'Readier for whatever life throws' cuts the idiom short (no 'at us'), uses an unusual word ('readier'), and widens 'challenges' to 'whatever'. The fix matches 'more equipped to deal with the challenges' in PMC12177368 and still lands on Ashtanga for slide 10 (12 words).
judged.final_line: One Ashtanga student said: practice makes me better at facing life's challenges.

verified.quote: Every day is a good day.
verified.original: 日日是好日 (rì rì shì hǎo rì). Case text: 舉雲門垂語云：「十五日已前不問汝，十五日已後道將一句來。」自代云：「日日是好日。」
verified.source: Blue Cliff Record (Biyan Lu 碧巖錄), case 6, compiled with commentary by Yuanwu Keqin, 1125. The English is a literal translation of the Chinese; no published translation was used.
verified.meaning: Every day, whatever it brings, is a good day.
verified.reason: I checked the Chinese on Wikisource (juan 1, 第六則), and it matches word for word. The case opens with 舉 ('Cited:'), and the item drops it, which is fine. The literal translation is accurate. Yuanwu's commentary does warn against shallow readings (後人只管隨語生解), so the item's caution is right. Blue Cliff case 16 is on the used list, but case 6 and Yunmen are not. SAFETY: use only the one line. The prose around the case includes Yunmen's foot being broken in a door, plus a ruler (廣主劉王) about to raise troops when Lingshu dies seated. Never quote or mention either story.

verified.quote: The contacts of matter, O son of Kuntî, giving cold and heat, pleasure and pain, they come and go, impermanent; endure them bravely, O Bhârata.
verified.original: मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः । आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत ॥ १४ ॥ (mātrā-sparśās tu kaunteya śītoṣṇa-sukha-duḥkha-dāḥ / āgamāpāyino 'nityās tāṁs titikṣasva bhārata)
verified.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14, tr. Annie Besant, The Bhagavad-Gita, 4th ed., 1922 (Wikisource transcription of the scanned edition, printed p. 24)
verified.meaning: Cold and heat, joy and pain come and go; meet them bravely.
verified.reason: I extracted the English and Sanskrit from the Wikisource page HTML and both match exactly. The page carries the 1922 date. Gita 2.14 is not on the used list (2.40, 2.47, 2.50, 4.34, 5.27, 6.16-17, 6.19, 6.23-25, 6.35, 6.40 and 18.37 are used). The trimmed slide form ending '...endure them bravely.' is faithful. Never mention the battlefield setting. The meaning line is faithful and under 14 words.

verified.quote: The misery which is not yet come is to be avoided.
verified.original: हेयं दुःखमनागतम् ॥१६॥ (heyaṁ duḥkham anāgatam)
verified.source: Yoga Sutra 2.16, tr. Swami Vivekananda, Raja Yoga (1896), in The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1 (Wikisource)
verified.meaning: Pain that has not come yet is the pain you can still avoid.
verified.reason: The sutra and English match the Wikisource page exactly. I also checked the Woods 1914 alternate in the archive.org text: 'That which is to be escaped is pain yet to come.' Vyasa's commentary in Woods says what the item claims: past pain cannot be escaped, present pain is already being felt, and 'only this pain [yet to come] becomes so changed that it may be escaped.' YS 2.16 is not on the used list. TONE: 'misery' is a heavy word, so frame the slide around getting ready early, never around danger.

verified.quote: Posture is that which is firm and pleasant.
verified.original: स्थिरसुखमासनम् ॥४६॥ (sthira-sukham āsanam)
verified.source: Yoga Sutra 2.46, tr. Swami Vivekananda, Raja Yoga (1896), in The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1 (Wikisource)
verified.meaning: Asana should be firm and steady, yet easy and pleasant too.
verified.reason: The sutra and English match exactly. Vivekananda's comment that follows ('Until you can get a firm seat you cannot practise the breathing...') confirms the item's honest limit: this is about a steady seat, not the Ashtanga sequence. I confirmed the Woods 1914 alternate, 'Stable-and-easy posture.', in the archive.org text. YS 2.46 is not on the used list (1.14, 1.21, 2.48 and 3.5 are). The idea is near the used Iyengar 'effortless ease' and Hatha Yoga Pradipika 1.17 lines, but the passage is different. I did not open the alternates Gita 3.8 or YS 3.46, so verify them separately before use.

verified.quote: Asana or posture gives Driddhata or strength; Mudra gives Sthirata or steadiness; Pratyahara gives Dhairyata or calmness; Pranayama gives lightness or Laghima.
verified.original: षट्कर्मणा शोधनञ्च आसनेन भवेद्दृढम् । मुद्रया स्थिरता चैव प्रत्याहारेण धीरता ॥ १० ॥ प्राणायामाल्लाघवञ्च ध्यानात्प्रत्यक्षमात्मनि । समाधिना निर्लिप्तञ्च मुक्तिरेव न संशयः ॥ ११ ॥ (read from the printed page image; āsanena bhaved dṛḍham, mudrayā sthiratā, pratyāhāreṇa dhīratā, prāṇāyāmāl lāghavam)
verified.source: Gheranda Samhita 1.10-11 (Lesson First), tr. Rai Bahadur Srisa Chandra Vasu, The Gheranda Samhita (Panini Office, Allahabad, 1914; Gheranda title page dated 1914), bound in Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. 15 (volume title page 1915), printed p. 3
verified.meaning: Asana builds strength, mudra steadiness, pratyahara calm, and pranayama lightness.
verified.credit: Gheranda Samhita 1.10-11 · tr. S. C. Vasu
verified.reason: I checked the printed page image (archive.org page n190, 'LESSON FIRST', p. 3). The book prints 'Driddhatâ', not 'Dridhata', so the quote must keep the printed spelling. The only other change is dropping the circumflexes (Âsana, Mudrâ, Pratyâhâra, Prânâyâma, Laghimâ), which is fine for a slide. The Gheranda title page in the scan is dated 1914, which matches the used-list citation; the combined volume is dated 1915. I added the Sanskrit, now legible in the image. Note that the Sanskrit says dhīratā for pratyahara, which Vasu renders as Dhairyata. Verse 9 ('Purificatory, strengthening, steadying, calming...') also checks out. Gheranda 1.5 and 1.8 are used, but 1.10-11 is a clearly different passage. Content is safe.

verified.quote: Though touched by worldly conditions, their mind does not tremble; sorrowless, stainless, secure: this is the highest blessing.
verified.original: Phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi, cittaṁ yassa na kampati; asokaṁ virajaṁ khemaṁ, etaṁ maṅgalamuttamaṁ.
verified.source: Sutta Nipata 2.4 (Mangala Sutta, 'Blessings'), segments 12.1-12.4, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral (CC0)
verified.meaning: A mind that stays steady through life's ups and downs is the best blessing.
verified.credit: The Buddha · Sutta Nipata 2.4, tr. Sujato
verified.reason: The Pali and English match the API segments 12.1-12.4 exactly. Leaving out the translation year is correct, since none was confirmed. The Mangala Sutta and Sutta Nipata are not on the used list. Content is safe. The next verse (13.2, 'undefeated everywhere') is not used. The meaning line is faithful and exactly 14 words.

verified.quote: Perform action, O Dhananjaya, dwelling in union with the divine, renouncing attachments and balanced evenly in success and failure: equilibrium is called yoga.
verified.original: योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय । सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते ॥ ४८ ॥ (yogasthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṁ tyaktvā dhanañjaya / siddhy-asiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṁ yoga ucyate)
verified.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.48, tr. Annie Besant, The Bhagavad-Gita, 4th ed., 1922 (Wikisource transcription of the scanned edition)
verified.meaning: Do your work and stay steady in success or failure; that steadiness is yoga.
verified.reason: The English and Sanskrit match the page exactly. Besant's footnote marker [25] sits after 'divine'; leave it out. Gita 2.48 is not used. The used '2.48' entry is Yoga Sutra 2.48, a different text. Gita 2.47 and 2.50 are used, but 2.48 is a distinct passage. Never mention the battlefield. The alternate Gita 2.56 also matches the same page ('free from anxiety amid pains... a sage of stable mind'). The meaning line is 14 words.

verified.quote: Earnest among the thoughtless, awake among the sleepers, the wise man advances like a racer, leaving behind the hack.
verified.original: Appamatto pamattesu, suttesu bahujāgaro; abalassaṁva sīghasso, hitvā yāti sumedhaso.
verified.source: Dhammapada 29 (ch. II, 'On Earnestness'), tr. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10, 1881 (Project Gutenberg eBook #2017)
verified.meaning: Stay wide awake while others doze, and you move ahead like a fast horse.
verified.credit: The Buddha · Dhammapada 29, tr. Max Müller
verified.reason: The text matches the Gutenberg file word for word, and the Pali matches the SuttaCentral dhp21-32 data. Dhammapada 29 is not used (19, 80, 81, 112, 204 and 239 are). Caveats: 'awake' means heedful, not early rising. 'Hack' (a tired, weak horse) will confuse translators, so gloss it as 'a slow horse' in the Thai, Chinese and Russian versions. The fit to stage E (daily repetition) is moderate, since the verse is about vigilance. The next verse (30) mentions Indra's lordship; do not use it.

verified.quote: Conditions fall apart. Persist with diligence.
verified.original: vayadhammā saṅkhārā, appamādena sampādetha.
verified.source: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), segment 6.7.3 (also 3.51.4), tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral, 2018 (CC0)
verified.meaning: Everything keeps changing, so keep practising with steady care.
verified.credit: The Buddha · Digha Nikaya 16, tr. Sujato
verified.reason: Both segments are confirmed in the API. 6.7.3 reads 'Conditions fall apart. Persist with diligence.' and 6.7.4 is 'These were the Realized One's last words.' The same line appears at 3.51.4. It is not on the used list. This is a peaceful death with no victims, so it does not break the rules. Still, keep 'last words' and the passing off the slide and credit (I shortened 'who' to 'The Buddha'). Frame the slide on change and steady practice. I tried to open the Rhys Davids 1881 SBE 11 rendering, but sacred-texts.com blocked the fetch, so do not use that alternate until it is checked.

verified.quote: By the practice of the different parts of Yogas the impurities being destroyed, knowledge becomes effulgent up to discrimination.
verified.original: योगाङ्गानुष्ठानादशुद्धिक्षये ज्ञानदीप्तिरा विवेकख्यातेः ॥२८॥ (yogāṅgānuṣṭhānād aśuddhi-kṣaye jñāna-dīptir ā viveka-khyāteḥ)
verified.source: Yoga Sutra 2.28, tr. Swami Vivekananda, Raja Yoga (1896), in The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1 (Wikisource)
verified.meaning: As you practise the limbs of yoga, impurity fades and clear knowing shines.
verified.reason: The sutra and English match exactly, including the plural 'Yogas' as printed. Sutra 2.29 ('...are the eight limbs of Yoga') and Vivekananda's comment 'It is first necessary to obtain physical and mental control.' are both on the same page, confirmed. Label the comment as Vivekananda's own words. The Woods 1914 alternate ('...enlightenment of perception reaching up to the discriminative discernment') is confirmed in the archive.org text. Not used. The wording is abstract for a slide, but it is accurate. Keep the Anusthana note to the word link only.

verified.quote: From that, the covering to the light of the Chitta is attenuated. The mind becomes fit for Dharana.
verified.original: ततः क्षीयते प्रकाशावरणम् ॥५२॥ धारणासु च योग्यता मनसः ॥५३॥ (tataḥ kṣīyate prakāśāvaraṇam; dhāraṇāsu ca yogyatā manasaḥ)
verified.source: Yoga Sutra 2.52-53, tr. Swami Vivekananda, Raja Yoga (1896), in The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1 (Wikisource)
verified.meaning: Breath practice clears the mind and makes it ready to focus.
verified.reason: Sutras 52 and 53 and Vivekananda's comments ('by Pranayama this covering is removed'; 'After this covering has been removed, we are able to concentrate the mind') match exactly. 'From that' refers to pranayama (2.49-51), so the meaning line is faithful. In the Woods 1914 text I confirmed 'For fixed-attentions also the central organ becomes fit' and the Vachaspati gloss 'restraint of breath steadies the central organ and makes it fit for fixed attentions'. Not used. The idea is close to the used Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.2 breath-and-mind line, but this is a different text. I shortened the credit to fit 45 characters.

verified.quote: Each morning, wake up. Do as much yoga as you want. Maybe you'll eat, maybe you'll fast. Maybe you'll sleep indoors, maybe you'll sleep outdoors... Practice yoga, and all is coming!
verified.original: "Yes," he replied. "Each morning, wake up. Do as much yoga as you want. Maybe you'll eat, maybe you'll fast. Maybe you'll sleep indoors, maybe you'll sleep outdoors. The next next morning, wake up. up. Do as much yoga as you want. Maybe you'll eat, maybe you'll fast. Maybe you'll sleep indoors, maybe you'll sleep outdoors. Practice yoga, and all is coming!" (web text as printed, with its copy glitch)
verified.who: K. Pattabhi Jois, as recalled by his student David Williams (Manju Jois translating)
verified.source: David Williams, 'Big Yogi, Little Yogi', in 'Remembrances of K. Pattabhi Jois', Yoga Journal (YJ Editors; datePublished 29 Oct 2009 in page metadata; page shows 'Updated January 14, 2025'). Conversation on the last night of Jois's 1975 visit to Encinitas, California.
verified.meaning: Wake up and practise each morning; whatever the day brings, all will come.
verified.credit: Pattabhi Jois · recalled by David Williams
verified.reason: Opened the page and matched the wording exactly, including the duplicated 'The next next morning, wake up. up.' glitch, which the '...' skips without changing the meaning. The page's structured data gives datePublished 2009-10-29. The setting (Encinitas, 1975, Manju translating) is on the page. This is a student's memory of spoken words through a translator, written about 34 years later. Always label it 'as recalled by David Williams', never as a Jois text. Content is safe and warm. It is not on the used list (the used Guardian 2009 item is a different line). Caution, not a rule breach: 'Practice and all is coming' is also the title of Remski's 2019 book on abuse in Ashtanga. Use only one of A1 and A11, since both come from the same page.

verified.quote: The sorrows and pleasure that result from any occurrences due to variations of time and place — to accept these with a peaceful, contented mind is santosha.
verified.original: 2. The sorrows and pleasure that result from any occurrences due to variations of time and place — to accept these with a peaceful, contented mind is santosha.
verified.source: Yoga Makaranda (Kannada ed. 1934; Tamil ed. 1938), ch. 2.1 'Yama and Niyama', niyama no. 2, p. 23; English tr. Lakshmi Ranganathan and Nandini Ranganathan (translators' note dated 15 Oct 2006), from the Tamil edition
verified.meaning: Good days and hard days both come; meet them with a calm, happy mind.
verified.reason: Downloaded the PDF and extracted the text. The wording matches exactly, the dash is in the source, and it is niyama no. 2. The running header (garbled font) decodes to '2.1. Yama and Niyama 23', so p. 23 is right. The title page gives Kannada 1934 and Tamil 1938. The translators' note is signed by Lakshmi and Nandini Ranganathan, October 15, 2006. This is a different passage from the used Yoga Makaranda 'divine nectar' line. Safe: no royalty, caste or fear in the quoted line (the caste reference is in niyama no. 1, which is not quoted). The meaning line is faithful. The terebess file is an unofficial host of the translators' free release.

verified.quote: Therefore, the body, sense organs, and mind must be stabilized to prevent obstacles ... from occurring.
verified.original: If the limbs and sub-limbs of yama and niyama are to be practiced, then steps should be taken to ensure that one does not fall victim to disease, obligation, or poverty. For when a person becomes ill, his mind cannot be steady, nor can he do any work. Therefore, the body, sense organs, and mind must be stabilized to prevent obstacles, such as disease, from occurring.
verified.source: Yoga Mala, end of the 'Niyama' chapter: the paragraph right after Ishwarapranidhana (Yoga Sutra 2.45), where asana is introduced, before the 'Pranayama' chapter. Written in Kannada 1958-c.1961, first published 1962; English tr. Sri Vishwanath Kadam and Dr. H. L. Chandrashekar, ed. Deirdre Summerbell; North Point Press 2002, new ed. 2010. Page not checked.
verified.meaning: Keep body, senses and mind steady so problems are stopped before they start.
verified.reason: The wording is exact in two copies of the 2010 text: the archive.org/download/YogaMala djvu OCR and terebess.hu/english/Yoga-Mala.pdf (both unofficial). The URL given is the official North Point 2010 lending record; its text is access-restricted, but its metadata confirms the 2010 edition and the chapters Yama, Niyama, Pranayama, Surya Namaskara and Yoga Asanas. The translators are named in the book's Acknowledgments. FIX: the source location. The 2010 contents have no 'Part One / asana section'; the passage closes the Niyama chapter. I also dropped the unverified '1999 first English ed.'. The ellipsis removes 'such as disease', which keeps the line clear of an illness scare without changing its sense. It is different from the used Yoga Mala 'intellectual power... Practice alone' passage (Pranayama chapter). Optional: drop the opening 'Therefore,' on the slide, with a leading '...'.

verified.quote: ...only by being prepared to suffer any obstacles that we may encounter along the way will we then accrue the desired benefits. If you leave it halfway, it is like falling down.
verified.original: Now I ask the reader to pay attention to what I am going to say. When we venture into some affair expecting a huge profit, only by being prepared to suffer any obstacles that we may encounter along the way will we then accrue the desired benefits. If you leave it halfway, it is like falling down. I ask you to bear the difficulty and pain that you may encounter.
verified.source: Yoga Makaranda (Kannada ed. 1934; Tamil ed. 1938), ch. 1.5 'Who has the authority to practise Yoga', p. 18; English tr. Lakshmi Ranganathan and Nandini Ranganathan, 2006
verified.meaning: Be ready to meet obstacles on the way, and do not stop halfway.
verified.reason: The wording, p. 18 and ch. 1.5 are confirmed in the extracted PDF text; the running header decodes to '18' and the section starts at p. 17. FIX: the meaning line. The old line ('you will reach the good things') left out the 'do not leave it halfway' half and implied a promise of good things. The new line is closer to the text. The quote is exact. It is weaker for the theme, because it is about persisting, not preparing in advance. 'Suffer' is a little heavy but not fear-based.
